source.title: N2G: A Scalable Approach for Quantifying Interpretable Neuron Representations in Large Language Models
source.authors: Alex Foote; Neel Nanda; Esben Kran; Ioannis Konstas; Fazl Barez

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses a different method—a graph representation of neuron activations—to illustrate a neuron with multiple distinct behaviors.
record.gate_note: The paper reports layerwise graph-prediction scores, but those measure how well N2G predicts neuron firing, not how prevalent polysemantic neurons are; they are not rows for these versions. The appendix explicitly describes one graph with three distinct phrase-related behaviors. Claims about neuron behavior from cited prior work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: This is a tool paper. Its results are N2G's accuracy at predicting neuron firing, by layer (Table 1). Polysemanticity appears only in one appendix figure (Fig. 4), described qualitatively, with no count, share or layer breakdown. That cannot bear on V2's prevalence claim or on any other version. The study relies on the concept (choosing SoLU to reduce polysemanticity) and reports only its own method's performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that N2G graphs capture neuron behaviour well in early layers but only partially in later layers. They attribute this to later-layer neurons responding to more abstract concepts across many contexts, and expect the problem to worsen in larger models. They note polysemanticity, when present, often appears as disconnected subgraphs, which may aid interpretation pending further experiments.
record.recipe_differences: N2G builds graphs from highly activating examples, token saliency, and augmented prompts; it does not reproduce the original neuron-analysis method.

fits_no_version.finding: In a SoLU language model, one neuron's N2G graph splits into three disconnected subgraphs, each a phrase in a different language (Dutch, English, Swedish). The authors say polysemanticity 'often shows up clearly' this way.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Polysemantic neurons persist in SoLU models and appear as disconnected subgraphs in activation-context graphs. This is qualitative and unquantified.

record.peer_reviewed: Published at ICLR 2023 Workshop on Trustworthy and Reliable Large-Scale Machine Learning Models
record.problems: The polysemanticity example is qualitative and limited to one illustrated neuron; the text gives neither its layer or neuron index nor a prevalence estimate. Experiments primarily use a SoLU model and top-activating examples.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's layerwise precision, recall, and F1 scores evaluate graph predictions against neuron firings, not polysemanticity itself, so they were not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: Prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons and its layer dependence; only one anecdotal neuron is shown.
All: no test of superposition as the cause.
No comparison of SoLU with other activations; the authors only speculate that typical activations give more complex graphs.
All: no analysis of whether the Dutch, English and Swedish behaviours share a feature.
All; the study restricts itself to top activations but does not compare activation ranges.

record.verdict_notes: The record's reader called this a T2 test, but the only polysemanticity evidence is one figure of one unnamed neuron, so I reclassified it as T4 with no verdicts. Table 1's layer trend measures graph prediction quality, not polysemanticity, and was correctly left out. The 'Table 4' in the text refers to Table 1.

versions.untested_parts: The prevalence of polysemantic neurons, including whether a large share of neurons show this behavior and whether its frequency differs by layer.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more features than there are neurons.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
Comparisons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization, and performance costs of reducing polysemanticity.
Whether the illustrated behaviors share a feature used by the model, or whether better tools show canonical polysemantic neurons to have one coherent job.
Whether polysemanticity classifications change across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: six-layer decoder-only Transformer model with SoLU activation
rows.operation_detail: Represented an example neuron's activating contexts as a graph and described its distinct subgraphs.
rows.measure: Qualitative neuron behavior represented by separate graph subgraphs
rows.value: Three distinct subgraphs associated with phrases in Dutch, English, and Swedish; the authors describe them as distinct behaviors.
rows.note: The text does not identify the layer or neuron index for this example. This is one illustrative neuron, not a prevalence estimate.
rows.check: A single illustrative neuron with no layer, index or prevalence figure cannot show whether 'a large share' of neurons are polysemantic, or how this varies by layer. 'Observed' overstates it. The subject is a SoLU model, which was chosen to reduce polysemanticity. This is an anecdote, not a measurement.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: R1 illustrates distinct behaviors in one neuron, but gives no estimate of how common this is or how prevalence varies by layer.
